content: Induction of labor is performed for various medical reasons and can be achieved through different methods. For women with low-risk pregnancies, certain methods of labor induction or cervical ripening may be appropriate for use in outpatient settings. This review aimed to evaluate the effectiveness, maternal satisfaction, healthcare costs, and safety of pharmacological and mechanical interventions for labor induction or cervical ripening in outpatient settings. The review included 34 studies involving 11 different methods of labor induction, with a total of 5003 women who were randomized. These women either received treatment at home or were discharged after initial treatment and monitoring in a hospital. The interventions studied included vaginal and intracervical prostaglandin E₂ (PGE₂), vaginal and oral misoprostol, isosorbide mononitrate, mifepristone, estrogens, amniotomy, and acupuncture. These were compared to placebo, no treatment, or routine care. Most trials involved healthy women with term pregnancies. The overall risk of bias in the studies was low or unclear, although blinding was either unclear or not attempted in 16 trials. The quality of evidence was generally graded as low to moderate. 1. Vaginal PGE₂ versus expectant management or placebo: Fewer women in the vaginal PGE₂ group required additional induction agents, but the confidence intervals were wide, indicating uncertainty in the results (RR 0.52, 95% CI 0.27 to 0.99; 150 women; 2 trials). There were no significant differences between groups in the rates of uterine hyperstimulation (with or without fetal heart rate changes) (RR 3.76, 95% CI 0.64 to 22.24; 244 women; 4 studies; low-quality evidence), cesarean section (RR 0.80, 95% CI 0.49 to 1.31; 288 women; 4 studies; low-quality evidence), or neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) admissions (RR 0.32, 95% CI 0.10 to 1.03; 230 infants; 3 studies; low-quality evidence). No data were available on outcomes such as vaginal birth within 24, 48, or 72 hours, hospital stay duration, emergency service use, maternal or caregiver satisfaction, or serious maternal and neonatal morbidity or mortality. 2. Intracervical PGE₂ versus expectant management or placebo: There was no significant difference in the need for additional induction agents (RR 0.98, 95% CI 0.74 to 1.32; 445 women; 3 studies), vaginal birth not achieved within 48 to 72 hours (RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.68 to 1.02; 43 women; 1 study; low-quality evidence), uterine hyperstimulation with fetal heart rate changes (RR 2.66, 95% CI 0.63 to 11.25; 488 women; 4 studies; low-quality evidence), cesarean section rates (RR 0.90, 95% CI 0.72 to 1.12; 674 women; 7 studies; moderate-quality evidence), or NICU admissions (RR 1.61, 95% CI 0.43 to 6.05; 215 infants; 3 studies; low-quality evidence). No uterine ruptures were reported in either the PGE₂ or placebo groups. Data on other outcomes, such as vaginal birth not achieved within 24 hours, hospital stay duration, emergency service use, maternal or caregiver satisfaction, or serious maternal and neonatal morbidity or mortality, were not available. 3. Vaginal misoprostol versus placebo: One small study reported no significant differences in perinatal death rates between groups, with no deaths in the treatment group and one stillbirth in the control group (RR 0.34, 95% CI 0.01 to 8.14; 77 infants; 1 study; low-quality evidence). There were no significant differences in uterine hyperstimulation with fetal heart rate changes (RR 1.97, 95% CI 0.43 to 9.00; 265 women; 3 studies; low-quality evidence), cesarean section rates (RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.61 to 1.46; 325 women; 4 studies; low-quality evidence), or NICU admissions (RR 0.89, 95% CI 0.54 to 1.47; 325 infants; 4 studies; low-quality evidence). No data were available on outcomes such as vaginal birth not achieved within 24, 48, or 72 hours, additional induction agents required, hospital stay duration, emergency service use, maternal or caregiver satisfaction, or serious maternal and neonatal morbidity or mortality. 4. Other findings: A small study found that women who received oral misoprostol were more likely to give birth within 24 hours (RR 0.65, 95% CI 0.48 to 0.86; 87 women; 1 study) and less likely to require additional induction agents (RR 0.60, 95% CI 0.37 to 0.97; 127 women; 2 studies). Women who received mifepristone were also less likely to require additional induction agents (average RR 0.59, 95% CI 0.37 to 0.95; 311 women; 4 studies; high heterogeneity). One trial each of acupuncture and outpatient amniotomy was included, but limited data were reported for these interventions. Conclusions: Labor induction in outpatient settings appears to be feasible, and serious adverse events are rare. However, there is insufficient evidence to determine the impact of these interventions on maternal or neonatal health. Some evidence suggests that outpatient induction agents may reduce the need for further interventions and shorten the time to birth compared to placebo or no treatment. There is a lack of data on maternal preferences, the most effective and safe methods, and cost-effectiveness. Further research is needed to compare various outpatient protocols and incorporate women's preferences into the design of these studies.
